findings.finding: The plan never specifies HOW _paged_search opts into rate-limit retry. The plan states 'opting that helper in covers all three [map readers]' but leaves ambiguous whether _paged_search (a) always calls _call_logged(rate_limit_retry=True) unconditionally, or (b) accepts and forwards a rate_limit_retry flag from its callers. These have opposite failure modes: (a) silently grants retry to any future caller that uses _paged_search for a non-safe purpose; (b) requires all three map-reader callers to thread the flag, but the plan's opt-in table lists only _paged_search as the opt-in site and does not list the callers — implying (a). An implementer choosing (a) ships a mechanism that violates the 'opt-in defaults to False' invariant the plan considers load-bearing for safety.
findings.location: Approach section — 'THE EXACT OPT-IN SITES' table, `_paged_search` row; also 'get_issuelinks_map (`:455`), get_parent_map (`:567`) and get_comment_map (`:469`) need NO site of their own'
findings.suggested_fix: The cleanest resolution given the plan's safety-by-default invariant: _paged_search is a reads-only helper (it only fetches, never writes), so it is safe to have it always call _call_logged(rate_limit_retry=True) unconditionally. State this explicitly: '_paged_search always passes rate_limit_retry=True to _call_logged because it is a reads-only pager; any caller that uses _paged_search for non-read purposes would be a design error, not an implicit retry grant.' Add this constraint to the docstring and assert it in the extraction-is-behaviour-preserving test.

findings.checklist_item: - [ ] Resolve the contradiction between 'mirror dispatch_one.py:150-171' (which does NOT jitter the Retry-After value) and 'jitter-then-clamp' (which does): either update the Approach to state that the DC path INTENTIONALLY adds jitter that the Cloud path omits (citing the Atlassian 'up to 20%' guidance as the reason), or update the AC to match the no-jitter prior-art model and explain why jitter is waived.
evidence: dispatch_one.py:157-166 (verified in repo): `if exc.code == 429: retry_after = parse_retry_after(...)`; then `delay: float = min(MAX_BACKOFF_S, retry_after)` — no jitter added to the header value in the existing path.

Atlassian docs (8.21 through 11.3, verified): 'Consider increasing the timeout by a random fraction, up to 20%' — jitter on the header value IS the Atlassian recommendation, so the prior-art path in dispatch_one.py is itself non-compliant with the Atlassian guidance; the DC implementation should add jitter but the plan does not explain this departure from the model.
findings.finding: S2's plan directs the implementer to both 'mirror' dispatch_one.py:150-171 (the existing prior-art 429 path, which applies no jitter to the Retry-After value — it uses `min(MAX_BACKOFF_S, retry_after)` directly) AND to 'apply jitter-then-clamp', which the AC then tests for. These are contradictory: following the cited model produces no jitter on the header path; following the plan's stated behaviour departs from the model. An implementer will either fail the AC (if they mirror the code) or silently diverge from the prior-art path (if they add jitter) without an explanation of why this path should differ.

evidence: Partially-verified: `parse_retry_after` and `MAX_BACKOFF_S` exist in `_errors.py` and are imported in `dispatch_one.py:37,41` — confirmed.

Unverified: the attribute path on `jira.exceptions.JIRAError` that exposes the `Retry-After` response header is never stated in either plan. The jira library typically provides `JIRAError.response` (a `requests.Response`), but this is not confirmed by either plan.

Contradicted relative to existing pattern: `dispatch_one.py:158-159` reads `exc.headers.get('Retry-After')` from `urllib.error.HTTPError`, not from `JIRAError`. The DC 429 case uses `JIRAError`, a different type.
`_as_backend_http_error` in `transport.py:176-194` reads only `.status_code` from `JIRAError`, confirming headers are not currently accessed from it anywhere in the DC transport.

findings.finding: S2 plans to call `parse_retry_after` with a `Retry-After` header value extracted from a `JIRAError`, but neither the parent plan nor S2 states or verifies how to access that header from `JIRAError`. The existing `_with_connection_retry` only reads `.status_code` from `JIRAError` (via `_as_backend_http_error`); the header access path (likely `exc.response.headers.get('Retry-After')` on `jira`'s `requests.Response`-backed exception) is a new integration surface that is unconfirmed. The already-used analogous path in `dispatch_one.py` uses `urllib.error.HTTPError.headers.get('Retry-After')` — a different object with different attributes. If `JIRAError.response` is None or absent (e.g. on a connection-level 429 from a proxy), the access silently returns None and jitter-backoff takes over; but if the attribute shape is wrong the 429 branch raises AttributeError instead of retrying.

scenarios: Implementer writes `exc.headers.get('Retry-After')` by analogy with the urllib path, but `JIRAError` has no `.headers` attribute — raises AttributeError at runtime on every DC 429.

Implementer writes `exc.response.headers.get('Retry-After')` correctly, but this is never verified against the installed `jira` library version, and a proxy-generated 429 (no `requests.Response`) causes `exc.response` to be None — AttributeError instead of graceful degradation.
findings.suggested_fix: In S2's Approach, add: 'The `Retry-After` header is read as `getattr(getattr(exc, "response", None), "headers", {}).get("Retry-After")` — guards against `response=None` (proxy-generated 429s) and does not use `exc.headers` (which `JIRAError` does not carry, unlike `urllib.error.HTTPError`). Verified against `jira.exceptions.JIRAError` in the installed `jira` library.' Also add an AC that the header-access path is verified or explicitly marked as gracefully degrading.

findings.finding: The plan's opt-in table asserts `_paged_search` routes through `_call_logged` (table column 'wrapper: _call_logged'), making the `rate_limit_retry=True` flag reachable for the three map readers (`get_issuelinks_map`, `get_parent_map`, `get_comment_map` paging). However, 9263's plan text — the only evidence available — says only 'add `_paged_search` and route the three whole-project readers through it.' It does not specify that `_paged_search` itself calls `_call_logged` rather than bare `_with_connection_retry`. If 9263 implements `_paged_search` with a direct `_with_connection_retry` call, the forwarding mechanism cannot carry `rate_limit_retry=True` to `_paged_search` through `_call_logged`'s flag — and the plan would need `_paged_search` to also accept and forward the parameter.
findings.location: Approach section, opt-in table row for `_paged_search`; prerequisite ticket rebar:9263-b404-cb6c-463f
findings.suggested_fix: Add a concrete cross-story constraint: the plan should specify that `_paged_search` MUST accept and forward `rate_limit_retry`, OR confirm (by reading 9263's merged diff) that it routes through `_call_logged`. Add an AC: 'Confirm `_paged_search` either routes through `_call_logged` (enabling flag forwarding) or itself accepts `rate_limit_retry=False`; verify by reading the post-9263 source before implementing the opt-in table.'

findings.finding: The mutation-per-member AC uses 'create_issue, add_comment, add_label, …' with an ellipsis, but the transport has at least 10 distinct mutation call sites that do NOT opt in: update_issue (two direct _with_connection_retry calls at :367-368), _assign (:382), transition_issue_by_name write leg (:400), set_relationship (:434), delete_issue (_call_logged path), delete_issue_link (_call_logged path), remove_label (two _call_logged calls), set_reporter (two _call_logged calls), set_parent (two _call_logged calls), set_issue_property/_put_property (_call_logged), set_entity_property/_put_property (_call_logged). The AC says 'driven per-member, since this is the duplicate-risk boundary and a single representative call would not prove the others are safe' — but the named members are only three of the ~12 distinct mutation entry points. An implementer following only the named list would leave the remaining mutations untested for the non-retry guarantee.
findings.location: AC: 'a 429 on a MUTATION (create_issue, add_comment, add_label, …) is NOT retried — it raises exactly as today, asserted per-member'
findings.suggested_fix: Replace the ellipsis in the mutation AC with the full explicit member list drawn from the current transport.py, matching the approach section's own language: 'driven per-member, since this is the duplicate-risk boundary'.

findings.finding: The plan never specifies what exception type `_with_connection_retry` raises when the 429-retry cap is exhausted. Two choices exist and both have correctness consequences: (a) re-raise the raw `JIRAError` — which escapes the adapter boundary the `_as_backend_http_error` translation exists to seal, leaking a vendor type to callers that catch only `BackendHTTPError`; (b) raise `BackendHTTPError(429)` — which is swallowed and misclassified by `probe_remote`'s `except BackendHTTPError` at transport.py:477, silently returning a probe result rather than surfacing rate-limit exhaustion. The plan explicitly states the translation invariant ('the intercept MUST see the raw JIRAError, BEFORE _as_backend_http_error translates it') but is silent on what happens once retries are exhausted, leaving the implementer to make a load-bearing choice with no stated requirement.
findings.location: Approach section — 'The ordering invariant that makes the mechanism possible at all'; 'Bounds' (retry cap); transport.py:267 (_as_backend_http_error raise) and transport.py:477 (probe_remote except BackendHTTPError)
findings.suggested_fix: Specify that cap-exhaustion raises `BackendHTTPError` with the 429 status code (translated, preserving the adapter boundary), and add a note that `probe_remote` should detect code==429 in its `except BackendHTTPError` block and re-raise rather than classifying it as an absence-probe result — since a rate-limit exhaustion is not a meaningful probe outcome.

findings.finding: The AC states 'asserted by grep showing neither [parse_retry_after nor MAX_BACKOFF_S] is restated in retry.py' but the proving commands section contains no such grep. The pytest run cannot verify absence of a redefinition — it would still pass if retry.py imported AND redefined the constant or parser. The AC promises a grep-based proof that is missing from the runbook.
findings.location: AC 'parse_retry_after and MAX_BACKOFF_S are IMPORTED AND USED'; Proving commands section (no corresponding command present)
findings.suggested_fix: Append to the proving commands: `grep -En 'MAX_BACKOFF_S[[:space:]]*=' src/.../retry.py | grep -v import && echo FAIL || echo OK` and similarly for `def parse_retry_after` — both should produce no output (exit 1 from grep = pass).

findings.finding: The plan specifies that a 429 on a mutation raises BackendHTTPError 'exactly as today', but it does not specify what exception type propagates to the caller when a READ exhausts the retry cap. If cap-exhaustion re-raises the raw JIRAError rather than translating it to BackendHTTPError, callers of read methods (which today only ever see BackendHTTPError for HTTP errors) will encounter an unexpected exception type and their existing error-handling branches will not fire.
findings.location: Bounds section ('a persistently rate-limited instance must fail loudly'); Mutations section ('translates to BackendHTTPError exactly as today'); AC: 'the cap exhausted' WARNING asserted
findings.suggested_fix: In the retry loop's cap-exhaustion branch, call `raise _as_backend_http_error(exc)` (the same helper mutations use) rather than `raise exc`, and add to the test matrix: 'a read that exhausts the cap raises BackendHTTPError, not JIRAError'.

findings.finding: The ADR deliverable is specified as 'a short ADR (or an amendment to ADR-0036)' — the disjunction leaves the artifact form undefined and delegates the choice to the executor. The two options differ in file path, numbering convention, and what a reader consulting ADR-0036 would find. The proving command (`ls docs/adr | grep -iE 'retry|rate.?limit|0036'`) accepts either form and does not verify that a reader of ADR-0036 is actually directed to the 429 policy (e.g. via an amendment note in ADR-0036 itself). The AC says 'a reader consulting ADR-0036 must not have to discover the 429 exception from a code comment' but neither the proving command nor the deliverable form ensures this navigation path.
findings.location: Scope: 'docs/adr/ — a short ADR (or an amendment to ADR-0036)'; AC: 'the divergence from ADR-0036 is recorded in an ADR (or an amendment)'
findings.suggested_fix: State: 'Create a new ADR-NNNN and add a one-line forward-reference in ADR-0036 pointing to it.' Then add `grep -c '429\|rate.limit\|ADR-' docs/adr/0036-*.md` asserting count >= 1 to verify the cross-reference exists.

findings.finding: ADR-0036 itself is not required to be amended or cross-referenced to the new 429 policy ADR. The proving commands only verify that a new file in docs/adr/ exists and contains '429'; they do not verify that ADR-0036 is updated with a forward-pointer. A developer consulting ADR-0036 as the authoritative retry reference will find no mention of the 429 exception and the per-failure-type split — the exact navigability gap the plan warns against ('A reader consulting ADR-0036 must not have to discover the 429 exception from a code comment').
findings.location: Scope section ('docs/adr/'); Acceptance criteria last bullet; Proving commands ('ls docs/adr | grep ...')
findings.suggested_fix: Add to the Proving commands section: `grep -n '429\|rate.limit\|retry.py' docs/adr/ADR-0036-*.md` (exact filename as appropriate). Require the ADR deliverable to be a documented amendment to ADR-0036 (preferred) or to include an explicit cross-reference back-patch to ADR-0036 so the original doc is not stranded.
